warnings: Quiz language appears sparse; make assessment prompts explicit.

improvement_notes: Clarify near the beginning that an encoder may be mounted on the wheel, motor shaft, or gearbox output; if it is not directly on the wheel, the gear ratio must be included in the ticks-to-wheel-motion conversion.

State explicitly that the midpoint-heading pose update is an approximation for short intervals, and optionally show the exact differential-drive arc update for advanced learners. The current implementation is pedagogically appropriate but should not be mistaken for an exact general solution.
Add a brief installation or execution note for matplotlib so beginners know how to run the Python lab in a standard environment.

Define whether a 'tick' means a pulse, edge, or decoded quadrature count before using the terms interchangeably. The lesson acknowledges counting-method variation, but a single concrete example would reduce residual ambiguity.

The lesson is strong but lengthy for a foundational class. The illustrator guidance under 'See It in Your Head' partially repeats the generated diagrams and could be shortened or moved into an instructor note.
The square challenge would be more actionable if it supplied one worked 90-degree turn calculation, such as equal-and-opposite wheel distances of Bπ/4 for an in-place turn.
The visual plan is relevant and well placed, but the hardware concept would benefit from one clearly labeled photograph showing an encoder, wheel, shaft, and counting pattern.

linkedin.title: How Robot Encoders Turn Wheel Motion into an Estimated Pose
linkedin.description: A practical robotics lesson on encoder ticks, wheel distance, differential-drive odometry, Python simulation, and why wheel-based position estimates drift.
linkedin.commentary:
A robot cannot navigate reliably by sensing the outside world alone. It also needs to estimate what its wheels have done.

This Professor OS lesson introduces that bridge from measurement to motion:

• Convert encoder ticks into wheel angle and distance.
• Compare left and right wheel travel to estimate straight motion, turning, and rotation in place.
• Use a midpoint-heading update to simulate differential-drive odometry in Python.
• Investigate why slip, unequal wheels, backlash, timing, and calibration errors cause drift.

The lesson combines equations, a worked RoboRover example, executable assertions, a plotted simulation, prediction questions, and a square-path challenge. Students are asked to predict each motion before running the code, making the simulation a test of reasoning rather than a decorative output.

Try the lab, change one wheel’s tick count, and observe how a small asymmetry changes the estimated path.
